claim: Tamoxifen therapy can decrease the incidence of breast cancer recurrence by up to 40%
source: As an adjuvant, tamoxifen therapy can decrease the incidence of breast cancer recurrence by up to 40% (Davies et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Davies et al., 2011

claim: Reduction of breast cancer recurrence persists for at least 10 years of continuous tamoxifen treatment
source: This exceptionally effective therapy remains standard of care for people with hormone-responsive cancers, and reduction of recurrence persists for at least 10 years of continuous tamoxifen treatment (Davies et al., 2013; Chlebowski et al., 2014; Gierach et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Davies et al., 2013; Chlebowski et al., 2014; Gierach et al., 2017

claim: Tamoxifen therapy has been associated with increased risk for hot flashes
source: In contrast to these benefits, tamoxifen therapy has been associated with a variety of negative side effects, including increased risk for hot flashes (Love et al., 1991; Howell et al., 2005; Francis et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Love et al., 1991; Howell et al., 2005; Francis et al., 2015

claim: Tamoxifen therapy has been associated with increased risk for endometrial cancer and venous thromboembolic events
source: endometrial cancer and venous thromboembolic events (Fisher et al., 1998; Cuzick et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to Fisher et al., 1998; Cuzick et al., 2007

claim: Tamoxifen therapy has been associated with bone loss
source: bone loss (Powles et al., 1996)
evidence: Supported by citation to Powles et al., 1996

claim: Tamoxifen therapy has been associated with fatigue
source: and fatigue (Haghighat et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citation to Haghighat et al., 2003

claim: Approximately 25% of eligible patients fail to start or complete tamoxifen therapy due to side effects and safety concerns
source: Accordingly, ~25% of eligible patients fail to start or complete this life-saving therapy due to side effects and safety concerns (Friese et al., 2013; Berkowitz et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Friese et al., 2013; Berkowitz et al., 2021

claim: ERα signaling regulates body temperature through distinct neuronal populations
source: Estrogen receptor alpha (ERα) signaling regulates body temperature (Bowe et al., 2006; Musatov et al., 2007; Mittelman-Smith et al., 2012; Martínez de Morentin et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bowe et al., 2006; Musatov et al., 2007; Mittelman-Smith et al., 2012; Martínez de Morentin et al., 2014

claim: ERα signaling regulates physical activity through distinct neuronal populations
source: physical activity (Musatov et al., 2007; Correa et al., 2015; van Veen et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to Musatov et al., 2007; Correa et al., 2015; van Veen et al., 2020

claim: ERα signaling regulates bone density through distinct neuronal populations
source: and bone density (Farman et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016; Herber et al., 2019) through distinct neuronal populations.
evidence: Supported by citations to Farman et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016; Herber et al., 2019

claim: Tamoxifen administration leads to changes in food intake and body weight in mice
source: Indeed, the hypothalamus-POA is a demonstrated target of tamoxifen, leading to changes in food intake and body weight (Wade and Heller, 1993; López et al., 2006; Lampert et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Wade and Heller, 1993; López et al., 2006; Lampert et al., 2013

claim: Tamoxifen administration leads to changes in the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis
source: and changes in the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (Wilson et al., 2003; Aquino et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Wilson et al., 2003; Aquino et al., 2016

claim: Tamoxifen administration leads to changes in the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axes
source: and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (Wilson et al., 2003) axes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wilson et al., 2003

claim: Tamoxifen administration blocks the estrogen dependent induction of the progesterone receptor in the ventromedial hypothalamus
source: Tamoxifen has also been shown to affect gene expression in the hypothalamus; its administration blocks the estrogen dependent induction of the progesterone receptor (Pgr) in the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH)
evidence: Supported by citations to Patisaul et al., 2003; Aquino et al., 2016; Sá et al., 2016

claim: Tamoxifen administration increases the expression of estrogen receptor beta in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus
source: and increases the expression of estrogen receptor beta (Esr2) in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVH) (Patisaul et al., 2003; Aquino et al., 2016; Sá et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Patisaul et al., 2003; Aquino et al., 2016; Sá et al., 2016

claim: Tamoxifen-treated mice showed significantly lower core body temperature compared to controls
source: Similarly, tamoxifen-treated mice showed significantly lower core body temperature compared to controls, as indicated by 24 hr averages from the last week of treatment (Sidak's Post-hoc: 24 hr p=0.0076, see Supplementary file 2 for detailed statistics).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis (p=0.0076)

claim: The difference in core body temperature between tamoxifen-treated and control mice is detected during the light phase when the animals are generally inactive
source: This difference is detected during the light phase when the animals are generally inactive (Light: p=0.0003) but not in the dark phase (Dark: p=0.1164) when movement can also influence core temperature (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis (Light: p=0.0003, Dark: p=0.1164) and Figure 1B and C

claim: A higher heat loss index was observed in mice treated with tamoxifen compared to controls
source: We observed a higher HLI in mice treated with tamoxifen compared to controls (Figures 1D and E and 24 hr: p=0.005).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis (p=0.005) and Figures 1D and E

claim: Tail skin temperature was significantly higher in tamoxifen-treated mice compared to controls during light phase
source: Tail skin temperature also was significantly higher in tamoxifen-treated mice compared to controls during light phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B, Light: p=0.0231, Dark: p=0.0968).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis (Light: p=0.0231) and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: Mice treated with tamoxifen exhibited lower temperature above the intrascapular region directly apposed to BAT depots
source: In addition, mice treated with tamoxifen exhibited lower temperature above the intrascapular region directly apposed to BAT depots (Figure 1F and G, t = 3.255, df = 8, p=0.0116)
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis (t = 3.255, df = 8, p=0.0116) and Figure 1F and G

claim: Postmortem qPCR analysis of BAT revealed lower expression of Ucp1 following tamoxifen treatment
source: Accordingly, postmortem quantitative (q)PCR analysis of BAT revealed lower expression of genes associated with thermogenesis, uncoupling protein 1 (Ucp1) (t = 2.738, df = 16, p=0.0146)
evidence: Supported by experimental qPCR data with statistical analysis (t = 2.738, df = 16, p=0.0146)

claim: Postmortem qPCR analysis of BAT revealed lower expression of Adrb3 following tamoxifen treatment
source: and adrenergic receptor beta 3 (Adrb3) (t = 2.732, df = 16, p=0.0148) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Supported by experimental qPCR data with statistical analysis (t = 2.732, df = 16, p=0.0148) and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: Tamoxifen treatment shifts mouse temperature balance toward increased heat dissipation and decreased heat production
source: Together, these results indicate that tamoxifen treatment shifts mouse temperature balance toward increased heat dissipation and decreased heat production, consistent with the observations in humans experiencing hot flashes.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental measurements of temperature, heat loss index, and BAT gene expression

claim: Tamoxifen treatment is associated with greater bone volume ratios in both metaphysis and diaphysis of the femur
source: Here, micro-computed tomography (microCT) scans revealed that tamoxifen treatment is associated with greater bone volume ratios in both metaphysis (t = 7.322, df = 10, p<0.0001) and diaphysis (t = 3.557, df = 10, p=0.0052) of the femur (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by microCT data with statistical analysis (metaphysis: t = 7.322, df = 10, p<0.0001; diaphysis: t = 3.557, df = 10, p=0.0052) and Figure 2A–C

claim: Tamoxifen treatment was associated with greater number and thickness, and less separation of trabecular bones in metaphysis
source: Tamoxifen treatment was also associated with greater number (t = 7.539, df = 10, p<0.0001) and thickness (t = 5.303, df = 10, p=0.0003), and less separation of trabecular bones (t = 7.331, df = 10, p<0.0001) in metaphysis (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by microCT data with statistical analysis and Figure 2B

claim: Bone mineral density and bone area in cortical bones were not significantly affected by tamoxifen treatment
source: Bone mineral density (t = 0.09262, df = 10, p=0.928) and bone area (t = 1.368, df = 10, p=0.2013) in cortical bones were not significantly affected by tamoxifen treatment (Figure 2C)
evidence: Supported by microCT data with statistical analysis showing no significant difference (BMD: p=0.928; bone area: p=0.2013) and Figure 2C

claim: Tamoxifen treatment was associated with significantly greater cortical thickness
source: however, tamoxifen treatment was associated with significantly greater cortical thickness (t = 2.451, df = 10, p=0.0342) (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: Supported by microCT data with statistical analysis (t = 2.451, df = 10, p=0.0342) and Figure 2A and C

claim: Chronic tamoxifen treatment increases bone mass in mice
source: Together, these data indicate that chronic tamoxifen treatment increases bone mass, consistent with previous studies showing increased bone formation and bone mass in mice following tamoxifen administration (Perry et al., 2005; Starnes et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to Perry et al., 2005; Starnes et al., 2007

claim: Tamoxifen resulted in a moderate decrease in 24 hr movement
source: In addition, tamoxifen resulted in a moderate decrease in 24 hr movement (t = 3.296, df = 42, p=0.006) (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Supported by telemetry data with statistical analysis (t = 3.296, df = 42, p=0.006) and Figure 2D and E

claim: Tamoxifen-treated mice did not show significant changes in body weight compared to control mice over 28 days of treatment
source: Tamoxifen-treated mice did not show significant changes in body weight compared to control mice, over 28 days of treatment (treatment: p=0.5468) (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements with statistical analysis (p=0.5468) and Figure 2F and G

claim: A total of 29,807 cells were analyzed by drop-Seq from hypothalamus-POA
source: A total of 29,807 cells (8220 from n = 3 vehicle-treated mice, 21,587 from n = 5 tamoxifen-treated mice) clustered into nine distinct cell types
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data

claim: Hypothalamus-POA cells clustered into nine distinct cell types: astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, neurons, endothelial cells, microglia, polydendrocytes, ependymal cells, mural cells, and fibroblasts
source: clustered into nine distinct cell types, annotated based on high expression of previously characterized cell-type markers (Moffitt et al., 2018; Saunders et al., 2018): astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, neurons, endothelial cells, microglia, polydendrocytes, ependymal cells, mural cells, and fibroblasts (UMAP: Figure 3A, tSNE: Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, cluster defining marker expression: Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data, citations to Moffitt et al., 2018; Saunders et al., 2018, and Figure 3A

claim: Gper1 transcripts were predominantly found in Mural cells
source: While neither Esr1, Esr2, nor the Esr1 target gene Pgr showed strong enrichment in any particular cell type (Figure 3B), Gper1 transcripts were predominantly found in Mural cells (LogFC: 1.39 compared to all other cell types, adj. p<1e-128).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data with statistical analysis (LogFC: 1.39, adj. p<1e-128) and Figure 3B

claim: Neurons and ependymal cells were most sensitive to tamoxifen administration, as indicated by the number of significantly induced and repressed genes
source: Among all cell types, neurons and ependymal cells were most sensitive to tamoxifen administration, as indicated by the number of significantly induced and repressed genes (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing differential expression analysis and Figure 3D

claim: Tamoxifen administration was associated with relatively few significant gene expression changes in mural cells
source: Although mural cells show significant enrichment of Gper1, tamoxifen administration was associated with relatively few significant gene expression changes in these cells (Figure 3D)
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing differential expression analysis and Figure 3D

claim: Tamoxifen administration induced a significant downregulation of genes involved in estrogen response in neurons, endothelial cells, and ependymal cells
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) using a gene set for estrogen response (GO:0043627) further identifies neurons and ependymal cells as markedly tamoxifen responsive: tamoxifen administration induced a significant downregulation of genes involved in estrogen response in neurons, endothelial cells, and ependymal cells (Figure 3E, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis and Figure 3E

claim: Tamoxifen treatment decreased the expression of genes annotated as targets of the proto-oncogene, Myc, in astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, neurons, endothelial cells, microglia, polydendrocytes, and ependymal cells
source: For example, tamoxifen treatment decreased the expression of genes annotated as targets of the proto-oncogene, Myc, in astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, neurons, endothelial cells, microglia, polydendrocytes, and ependymal cells.
evidence: Supported by GSEA pathway analysis

claim: Neuronal sub-clustering resulted in 25 apparent neuronal subtypes
source: Neuronal sub-clustering resulted in 25 apparent neuronal subtypes (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing clustering analysis and Figure 4A

claim: Esr1 expression was significantly enriched in wild-type neurons expressing the neuropeptide precursor, Tac2
source: Esr1 expression was observed in various neuronal subclusters (Figure 4B), but was significantly enriched in wild-type neurons expressing the neuropeptide precursor, Tac2 (log2FC = 1.52, adj. p=7.1e-36)
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data with statistical analysis (log2FC = 1.52, adj. p=7.1e-36) and Figure 4B

claim: Esr1 expression was significantly enriched in neurons expressing the neuropeptide precursor Gal
source: and neurons expressing the neuropeptide precursor Gal (log2FC = 0.50, adj. p=1.6e-30) compared to all other neuronal subclusters.
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data with statistical analysis (log2FC = 0.50, adj. p=1.6e-30)

claim: The ERα target gene Pgr was significantly enriched in wild-type neurons expressing Tac2
source: The ERα target gene Pgr also was significantly enriched in wild-type neurons expressing Tac2 (log2FC = 0.49, adj. p=2.3e-4) compared to all other neuronal subclusters.
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data with statistical analysis (log2FC = 0.49, adj. p=2.3e-4)

claim: Tamoxifen administration is associated with a significant down-regulation of genes involved in neuropeptide signaling in neurons
source: GSEA demonstrates that overall, tamoxifen administration is associated with a significant down-regulation of genes involved in neuropeptide signaling, a critical aspect of neuronal function
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis

claim: Tamoxifen administration is associated with a significant down-regulation of genes involved in oxidative phosphorylation in neurons
source: as well as the two principal components fueling the sizeable energy demands of neuronal metabolism: oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis (Yellen, 2018; Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis, citation to Yellen, 2018, and Figure 4C

claim: Tamoxifen administration is associated with a significant down-regulation of genes involved in glycolysis in neurons
source: as well as the two principal components fueling the sizeable energy demands of neuronal metabolism: oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis (Yellen, 2018; Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis, citation to Yellen, 2018, and Figure 4C

claim: ERα immunoreactivity was clearly ablated in several areas of the hypothalamus-POA of Esr1 cKO mice, including the medial preoptic area, ventrolateral subdivision of the ventromedial nucleus of the hypothalamus, and arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus
source: Most importantly, ERα immunoreactivity was clearly ablated in several areas of the hypothalamus-POA of Esr1 cKO mice, including the medial preoptic area (MPA), ventrolateral subdivision of the ventromedial nucleus of the hypothalamus (VMHvl), and arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus (ARC) (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data and Figure 5A

claim: Tamoxifen treatment led to significant transcriptional changes in the hypothalamus-POA of Esr1 cKO mice
source: Interestingly, tamoxifen treatment led to significant transcriptional changes in the hypothalamus-POA of Esr1 cKO mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing differential expression analysis and Figure 5B

claim: There was a strong negative Spearman correlation observed in most cell types when comparing tamoxifen-induced gene expression changes in wild-type versus Esr1 cKO cells
source: For this gene-by-gene comparison, there was a strong negative Spearman correlation observed in most cell types (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis and Figure 5C

claim: The majority of significant tamoxifen-induced gene expression changes observed in cell types of wild-type female mice were ablated or regulated in the opposite direction in Esr1 cKO animals
source: This negative correlation implies that the majority of significant tamoxifen-induced gene expression changes that were observed in cell types of wild-type female mice were ablated or regulated in the opposite direction in Esr1 cKO animals.
evidence: Inferred from the negative Spearman correlation analysis

claim: In wild-type neurons, the majority of tamoxifen-regulated genes were repressed by tamoxifen
source: In wild-type neurons, the majority of tamoxifen-regulated genes were repressed by tamoxifen (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing differential expression analysis and Figure 3D

claim: In Esr1 cKO neurons, most of the genes repressed by tamoxifen in wild-type are no longer repressed by tamoxifen
source: In Esr1 cKO neurons, most of these same genes are no longer repressed by tamoxifen (Figure 5D, Key: Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing differential expression analysis and Figure 5D

claim: In wild-type ependymal cells, the majority of regulated genes were induced by tamoxifen
source: In wild-type ependymal cells, the majority of regulated genes were induced by tamoxifen (Figure 3D)
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing differential expression analysis and Figure 3D

claim: The majority of genes induced by tamoxifen in wild-type ependymal cells were suppressed by tamoxifen in Esr1 cKO ependymocytes
source: and the majority of these same genes were suppressed by tamoxifen in Esr1 cKO ependymocytes (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing differential expression analysis and Figure 5D

claim: Tamoxifen downregulated estrogen responsive genes in multiple cell types of the wild-type hypothalamus-POA but did not significantly affect the same gene set in cells of the Esr1 cKO hypothalamus-POA
source: GSEA for estrogen responsive genes in all cell types showed that tamoxifen downregulated estrogen responsive genes in multiple cell types of the wild-type hypothalamus-POA but did not significantly affect the same gene set in cells of the Esr1 cKO hypothalamus-POA, even when using a permissive cutoff for significance (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C, Supplementary file 1a and 1f).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C

claim: Both oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis were upregulated by tamoxifen in Esr1 cKO neurons
source: Importantly, we also found a significant change of metabolic gene expression in neurons, as both oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis were upregulated by tamoxifen in Esr1 cKO neurons (Figure 5E)
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis and Figure 5E

claim: Oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis were downregulated by tamoxifen in wild-type neurons
source: but downregulated in wild-type neurons (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis and Figure 4C

claim: The majority of tamoxifen-induced changes in gene expression in the hypothalamus-POA are dependent upon expression of ERα in the Nkx2-1 lineage
source: Together these data demonstrate that the majority of tamoxifen-induced changes in gene expression in the hypothalamus-POA are dependent upon expression of ERα in the Nkx2-1 lineage.
evidence: Inferred from multiple GSEA and differential expression analyses comparing wild-type and Esr1 cKO responses to tamoxifen

claim: Tamoxifen injection was not associated with any difference in core body temperature in Esr1 cKO mice compared to vehicle-treated controls
source: Interestingly, tamoxifen injection was not associated with any difference in core body temperature in Esr1 cKO mice compared to vehicle-treated controls (treatment: F(1, 14)=0.1395, p=0.7144) (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: Supported by telemetry data with statistical analysis (F(1, 14)=0.1395, p=0.7144) and Figure 6A–B

claim: No significant differences in heat dissipation were detected when comparing Esr1 cKO mice treated with tamoxifen vs. vehicle, as indicated by HLI
source: Specifically, we did not detect any significant differences in heat dissipation or production when comparing Esr1 cKO mice treated with tamoxifen vs. vehicle, as indicated by HLI (treatment: F(1, 13)=3.109, p=0.1013)
evidence: Supported by telemetry data with statistical analysis (F(1, 13)=3.109, p=0.1013)

claim: No significant differences in BAT temperature were detected when comparing Esr1 cKO mice treated with tamoxifen vs. vehicle
source: and BAT temperature (t = 0.2640, df = 4, p=0.8048) (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: Supported by thermal imaging data with statistical analysis (t = 0.2640, df = 4, p=0.8048) and Figure 6E–F

claim: There was no significant difference in movement between tamoxifen and vehicle treatment in Esr1 cKO mice
source: In contrast to wild-type mice, there was no significant difference in movement between tamoxifen and vehicle treatment in Esr1 cKO mice (treatment: F(1, 14)=2.638, p=0.1266) (Figure 6G–H).
evidence: Supported by telemetry data with statistical analysis (F(1, 14)=2.638, p=0.1266) and Figure 6G–H

claim: Knockout of ERα in the hypothalamus-POA largely blocked the effect of tamoxifen on bone physiology
source: Knockout of ERα in the hypothalamus-POA largely blocked the effect of tamoxifen on bone physiology as well.
evidence: Inferred from multiple bone measurements showing no significant differences in Esr1 cKO mice

claim: No difference was observed in bone volume fraction when comparing tamoxifen to vehicle-treated Esr1 cKO animals
source: No difference was observed in bone volume fraction (t = 0.8340, df = 10, p=0.4237)
evidence: Supported by microCT data with statistical analysis (t = 0.8340, df = 10, p=0.4237)

claim: No difference was observed in trabecular thickness when comparing tamoxifen to vehicle-treated Esr1 cKO animals
evidence: Supported by microCT data with statistical analysis (t = 0.2668, df = 10, p=0.7951)

claim: No difference was observed in trabecular separation when comparing tamoxifen to vehicle-treated Esr1 cKO animals
source: or separation of trabeculae (t = 1.924, df = 10, p=0.0832) when comparing tamoxifen to vehicle-treated animals.
evidence: Supported by microCT data with statistical analysis (t = 1.924, df = 10, p=0.0832)

claim: A tamoxifen-induced reduction in trabecular number was observed in Esr1 cKO mice
source: In contrast to wild-type mice, we observed a tamoxifen-induced reduction in trabecular number (t = 3.349, df = 10, p=0.0074) (Figure 6I–J).
evidence: Supported by microCT data with statistical analysis (t = 3.349, df = 10, p=0.0074) and Figure 6I–J

claim: There was no significant difference in bone volume ratio in the cortical bones of Esr1 cKO mice treated with tamoxifen compared to mice treated with vehicle
source: There was no significant difference in bone volume ratio (t = 0.5963, df = 10, p=0.5643)
evidence: Supported by microCT data with statistical analysis (t = 0.5963, df = 10, p=0.5643)

claim: There was no significant difference in cortical thickness in the cortical bones of Esr1 cKO mice treated with tamoxifen compared to mice treated with vehicle
source: or cortical thickness (t = 0.9720, df = 10, p=0.3540) in the cortical bones of mice treated with tamoxifen compared to mice treated with vehicle (Figure 6I and K).
evidence: Supported by microCT data with statistical analysis (t = 0.9720, df = 10, p=0.3540) and Figure 6I and K

claim: The dysregulation of core temperature, reduced movement, and changed bone physiology associated with tamoxifen treatment in wild-type mice are largely dependent upon the expression of ERα in the Nkx2-1 lineage
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the dysregulation of core temperature, reduced movement, and changed bone physiology associated with tamoxifen treatment in wild-type mice are largely dependent upon the expression of ERα in the Nkx2-1 lineage.
evidence: Inferred from multiple physiological measurements comparing wild-type and Esr1 cKO responses to tamoxifen

claim: Tamoxifen and its metabolites are detectable and up to 46-fold higher in the brain than in serum of breast cancer patients
source: Indeed, tamoxifen and its metabolites are detectable and up to 46-fold higher in the brain than in serum of breast cancer patients (Lien et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lien et al., 1991

claim: Tamoxifen treatment affects gene expression in many cell types but most strongly in neurons and ependymal cells
source: We report that tamoxifen treatment affects gene expression in many cell types but most strongly in neurons and ependymal cells.
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing differential expression analysis

claim: Tamoxifen treatment does not change the proportion of different cell types after 28 days of treatment with a clinically relevant dose
source: Although much higher doses, such as those used to activate tamoxifen-inducible mouse models (25–100 mg/kg), can inhibit neural progenitor cell proliferation during cortical patterning or induce adipogenesis and prolonged genetic effects (Ye et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2020), we do not detect any changes in the proportion of different cell types after 28 days of treatment with a clinically relevant dose (0.1 mg/kg) of tamoxifen.
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data and citations to Ye et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2020

claim: Conditional knockout of the Esr1 gene encoding ERα did not render the brain insensitive to tamoxifen
source: Notably, conditional knockout of the Esr1 gene encoding ERα did not render the brain insensitive to tamoxifen.
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data showing transcriptional changes in Esr1 cKO mice

claim: Conditional knockout of ERα in the hypothalamus-POA blocked the majority of the physiological changes observed in wild-type mice by tamoxifen
source: Nevertheless, conditional knockout of ERα in the hypothalamus-POA blocked the majority of the physiological changes observed in wild-type mice by tamoxifen, indicating a pivotal role of ERα in mediating the homeostatic effects of tamoxifen.
evidence: Supported by multiple physiological measurements in Esr1 cKO mice

claim: ERα plays an indispensable role in the molecular and physiological response to tamoxifen treatment in mice
source: Together, these data indicate an indispensable role for ERα in the molecular and physiological response to tamoxifen treatment in mice.
evidence: Inferred from combined transcriptomic and physiological data comparing wild-type and Esr1 cKO responses to tamoxifen

claim: Tamoxifen exerts potent effects on gene expression in a variety of neuronal subtypes, as well as in ependymal cells
source: In addition, our data indicate that tamoxifen exerts potent effects on gene expression in a variety of neuronal subtypes, as well as in ependymal cells.
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing differential expression analysis

claim: Activating neurons in the ARC that co-express kisspeptin, neurokinin B, and dynorphin induces hot flash-like symptoms in rodents and humans
source: Specifically, activating neurons in the ARC that co-express kisspeptin, neurokinin B, and dynorphin (KNDy neurons, which also express ERα) or manipulating their downstream neurokinin B signaling in the POA induces hot flash-like symptoms in rodents and humans (Dacks et al., 2011; Jayasena et al., 2015; Padilla et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dacks et al., 2011; Jayasena et al., 2015; Padilla et al., 2018

claim: Manipulating neurokinin B signaling in the POA induces hot flash-like symptoms in rodents and humans
source: Specifically, activating neurons in the ARC that co-express kisspeptin, neurokinin B, and dynorphin (KNDy neurons, which also express ERα) or manipulating their downstream neurokinin B signaling in the POA induces hot flash-like symptoms in rodents and humans (Dacks et al., 2011; Jayasena et al., 2015; Padilla et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dacks et al., 2011; Jayasena et al., 2015; Padilla et al., 2018

claim: Tamoxifen may interact with neurokinin B signaling through ERα in the ARC or the POA
source: We detected the highest Esr1 expression levels in neurons marked by expression of the neurokinin B precursor gene, Tac2, suggesting that tamoxifen may interact with neurokinin B signaling through ERα in the ARC or the POA.
evidence: Inferred from Esr1 expression data in Tac2 neurons and known roles of these neurons in hot flashes

claim: Esr1 cKO mice showed loss of ERα in the ARC and POA
source: Indeed, Esr1 cKO mice which showed loss of ERα in the ARC and POA (Figure 5A) did not exhibit tamoxifen-induced tail and core temperature changes.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data and Figure 5A

claim: Tamoxifen induces hot flashes via estrogen-sensitive neural circuits involved in thermoregulation
source: Together, these data suggest the hypothesis that tamoxifen induces hot flashes via estrogen-sensitive neural circuits involved in thermoregulation.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence including temperature measurements, ERα expression patterns, and Esr1 cKO phenotypes

claim: The sustained increase in tail skin temperature observed in animal models does not fully reflect the episodic nature of hot flashes in humans
source: However, it is important to acknowledge that the sustained increase in tail skin temperature observed here and in other animal models (Kobayashi et al., 2000; Padilla et al., 2018) does not fully reflect the episodic nature of hot flashes in humans.
evidence: Supported by comparison to other studies (Kobayashi et al., 2000; Padilla et al., 2018) and knowledge of human hot flash characteristics

claim: Treating ovariectomized rats with selective ligands for ERβ can mimic the effects of estradiol treatment on tail skin temperature
source: For example, treating ovariectomized rats with selective ligands for ERβ can mimic the effects of estradiol treatment on tail skin temperature (Opas et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Opas et al., 2009

claim: A Gq-coupled estrogen receptor ligand (STX) is able to decrease core body temperature similar to E2 in guinea pigs after ovariectomy
source: Similarly, a Gq-coupled estrogen receptor ligand (STX) is able to decrease core body temperature similar to E2 in guinea pigs after ovariectomy (Roepke et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Roepke et al., 2010

claim: Ablating ERα is sufficient to abrogate the effects of tamoxifen on core body temperature and tail skin temperature in mice
source: Although the effects of estrogens on thermoregulation are probably multifaceted and complex, it is clear that ablating ERα is sufficient to abrogate the effects of tamoxifen on core body temperature and tail skin temperature in mice.
evidence: Supported by temperature measurements in Esr1 cKO mice

claim: Estrogen signaling promotes movement in animal studies
source: Animal studies indicate that estrogen signaling promotes movement (Ogawa et al., 2003; Lightfoot, 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to Ogawa et al., 2003; Lightfoot, 2008

claim: There is a significant association between ongoing tamoxifen usage and symptoms of fatigue in female breast cancer patients
source: In female breast cancer patients, there is a significant association between ongoing tamoxifen usage and symptoms of fatigue (Haghighat et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Haghighat et al., 2003

claim: ERα in the hypothalamus-POA mediates a suppressive effect of tamoxifen on movement
source: Our results demonstrate that ERα in the hypothalamus-POA mediates a suppressive effect of tamoxifen on movement.
evidence: Supported by movement measurements in wild-type and Esr1 cKO mice

claim: ERα signaling in the hypothalamus-POA regulates physical activity in mice
source: This is consistent with the results that ERα signaling in the hypothalamus-POA regulates physical activity in mice (Ogawa et al., 2003; Musatov et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2011; Sano et al., 2013; Correa et al., 2015; van Veen et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ogawa et al., 2003; Musatov et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2011; Sano et al., 2013; Correa et al., 2015; van Veen et al., 2020

claim: Activation of ERα neurons in the Nkx2-1 lineage promotes movement
source: Specifically, activation of ERα neurons in the Nkx2-1 lineage promotes movement (Correa et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Correa et al., 2015

claim: Loss of ERα in the VMH reduces physical activity in mice
source: and loss of ERα in the VMH reduces physical activity in mice (Musatov et al., 2007; Correa et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Musatov et al., 2007; Correa et al., 2015

claim: The POA is rich in ERα expression and has been shown to be responsible for estrogen induced running wheel activity
source: In addition, the POA is rich in ERα expression and has been shown to be responsible for estrogen induced running wheel activity (King, 1979; Fahrbach et al., 1985; Takeo and Sakuma, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to King, 1979; Fahrbach et al., 1985; Takeo and Sakuma, 1995

claim: Physical activity is primarily regulated by ERα signaling in mice
source: Although ERβ also is expressed in the hypothalamus-POA, physical activity is primarily regulated by ERα signaling in mice (Ogawa et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ogawa et al., 2003

claim: Tamoxifen is protective against bone mineral density loss after menopause in humans
source: Human studies have demonstrated that tamoxifen is protective against bone mineral density loss after menopause but induces bone loss before menopause (Love et al., 1992; Kristensen et al., 1994; Powles et al., 1996; Vehmanen et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Love et al., 1992; Kristensen et al., 1994; Powles et al., 1996; Vehmanen et al., 2006

claim: Tamoxifen induces bone loss before menopause in humans
source: Human studies have demonstrated that tamoxifen is protective against bone mineral density loss after menopause but induces bone loss before menopause (Love et al., 1992; Kristensen et al., 1994; Powles et al., 1996; Vehmanen et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Love et al., 1992; Kristensen et al., 1994; Powles et al., 1996; Vehmanen et al., 2006

claim: Animal studies have generally shown protective effects of tamoxifen on bone, regardless of ovarian function
source: In contrast, animal studies have generally shown protective effects of tamoxifen on bone, regardless of ovarian function (Turner et al., 1988; Perry et al., 2005; Starnes et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Turner et al., 1988; Perry et al., 2005; Starnes et al., 2007

claim: Tamoxifen can stimulate bone formation
source: Although this study did not evaluate bone formation and resorption respectively, a number of animal studies have indicated that tamoxifen can stimulate bone formation (Perry et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citation to Perry et al., 2005

claim: Tamoxifen can suppress bone resorption
source: and also suppress bone resorption (Turner et al., 1988; Quaedackers et al., 2001)
evidence: Supported by citations to Turner et al., 1988; Quaedackers et al., 2001

claim: At least some of the effects of tamoxifen on bone are mediated by ERα signaling within the Nkx2-1 lineage
source: These results suggest that at least some of the effects of tamoxifen on bone are mediated by ERα signaling within the Nkx2-1 lineage.
evidence: Inferred from bone measurements in Esr1 cKO mice showing ablation of some tamoxifen effects

claim: E2 replacement after ovariectomy can increase cortical bone dimensions in ERα and ERβ double KO mice
source: Indeed, E2 replacement after ovariectomy can increase cortical bone dimensions in ERα and ERβ double KO mice (Lindberg et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lindberg et al., 2002

claim: A Gq-coupled estrogen receptor ligand is able to increase bone density in guinea pigs after ovariectomy
source: and a Gq-coupled estrogen receptor ligand is able to increase bone density in guinea pigs after ovariectomy (Roepke et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Roepke et al., 2010

claim: Depletion of ERα in the medial basal hypothalamus results in an impressive increase in bone mass
source: However, depletion of ERα in the medial basal hypothalamus or specifically within the KNDy neurons results in an impressive increase in bone mass (Farman et al., 2016; Herber et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to Farman et al., 2016; Herber et al., 2019

claim: Depletion of ERα specifically within the KNDy neurons results in an impressive increase in bone mass
source: However, depletion of ERα in the medial basal hypothalamus or specifically within the KNDy neurons results in an impressive increase in bone mass (Farman et al., 2016; Herber et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to Farman et al., 2016; Herber et al., 2019

claim: Conditional ERα ablation in the hypothalamus-POA can abrogate the effects of tamoxifen on bone volume
source: The potent effect of hypothalamic ERα on bone is consistent with our finding that conditional ERα ablation in the hypothalamus-POA can abrogate the effects of tamoxifen on bone volume.
evidence: Supported by bone measurements in Esr1 cKO mice

claim: Esr1 expression is not altered in the thyroid, pituitary, and lung of Esr1 cKO mice
source: Although the Nkx2-1 lineage includes cells in the thyroid, pituitary, and lung, Esr1 expression is not altered in these peripheral tissues of Esr1 cKO mice (Herber et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to Herber et al., 2019

claim: The hypothalamus-POA is the most likely mediator of the ERα-dependent physiological effects of tamoxifen
source: Although the Nkx2-1 lineage includes cells in the thyroid, pituitary, and lung, Esr1 expression is not altered in these peripheral tissues of Esr1 cKO mice (Herber et al., 2019), leaving the hypothalamus-POA as the most likely mediator of the ERα-dependent physiological effects of tamoxifen reported here.
evidence: Inferred from Esr1 expression patterns and physiological effects in Esr1 cKO mice

claim: Peripheral tissues are likely affected by systemic tamoxifen administration, leading to other physiological effects
source: Despite this, it is very likely that peripheral tissues are also affected by systemic tamoxifen administration, leading to other physiological effects that we did not examine.
evidence: Inferred from the systemic nature of tamoxifen administration and known effects in other tissues

claim: Estrogen suppression therapies, including tamoxifen or aromatase inhibitors, can lead to the dysregulation of energy balance and glucose homeostasis in humans and rodents
source: Indeed, there is evidence that estrogen suppression therapies, including tamoxifen or aromatase inhibitors, can lead to the dysregulation of energy balance and glucose homeostasis in humans and when modeled in rodents (López et al., 2006; Lampert et al., 2013; Ceasrine et al., 2019; Scalzo et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to López et al., 2006; Lampert et al., 2013; Ceasrine et al., 2019; Scalzo et al., 2020

claim: The rodent model of tamoxifen treatment mimics several of the key side effects of endocrine therapy observed in humans
source: In summary, the rodent model of tamoxifen treatment provided here mimics several of the key side effects of endocrine therapy observed in humans.
evidence: Supported by multiple physiological measurements in mice compared to known human side effects

claim: Tamoxifen treatment may alter thermoregulation, physical activity, and bone through ERα signaling in the brain
source: If translatable to humans, our findings suggest the hypothesis that tamoxifen treatment may alter thermoregulation, physical activity, and bone through ERα signaling in the brain.
evidence: Inferred from mouse data and speculated to apply to humans

claim: Women often experienced more of tamoxifen's side effects than men
source: A recent survey conducted in the online breast cancer communities showed that women often experienced more of tamoxifen's side effects than men and one-third of patients did not feel that their side effects were taken seriously (Berkowitz et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Berkowitz et al., 2021

claim: One-third of patients did not feel that their side effects were taken seriously
source: A recent survey conducted in the online breast cancer communities showed that women often experienced more of tamoxifen's side effects than men and one-third of patients did not feel that their side effects were taken seriously (Berkowitz et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Berkowitz et al., 2021
